# Independent audit: global intrinsic ball lift of normalized thin-fiber laws



## Support, mass, and density dimension

The fixed bounded region makes weak convergence preserve the individual finite masses, so the positive surviving weights sum to one after zero-weight indices are discarded. A positive limiting weight ensures that the corresponding prelimit fibers eventually have positive m-volume, allowing their conditional uniform laws to be defined.

For any x in the Hausdorff limit, the copy `(1-t)x_l+t K_l` occupies a uniform proportion t^m of K_l and lies in a prescribed closed ball about x for a fixed sufficiently small t. Upper Portmanteau gives positive limiting mass in that ball. Repeating at smaller radii proves equality of the weak support and the complete Hausdorff fiber limit, including exposed points. The reverse inclusion follows directly from Hausdorff convergence. The Portmanteau direction is correct.

Since every prelimit fiber volume is at most M_l and M_l tends to zero, Hausdorff volume continuity forces its limit dimension q_z to be less than m. The companion Borell result therefore gives density-root exponent 1/(m-q_z) on the support affine plane, or a Dirac mass when q_z=0. Neither exponent m-q_z nor the relative mass p_z is replaced by an independently normalized probability density during the lift construction.

## Every anchored incidence has one common direction space

For a positive source with coefficient lambda in a representation of integer target j, actual compatibility supplies a translated copy of lambda K_(z,l) in K_(j,l). Positive source relative mass bounds the target/source volume ratio. The elementary maximum-simplex normalization and cone-volume argument then bound every target width above by a fixed multiple of the source width; containment gives the reverse inequality. Passing to Hausdorff limits proves identical direction spaces, not merely equal dimensions.

The stated width constant has the correct normalization: after translating, B' contains lambda times the unit ball; a cone from any v in B' to the perpendicular radius-lambda disk has volume `kappa_(m-1)lambda^(m-1)|v|/m`. The same formula is valid at m=1 with H_0 of the disk equal to one. The fixed inner ball in A' converts the resulting diameter estimate to the stated directional-width bound.

All source and target affine supports in a given anchored combination are therefore parallel and have the same dimension. The limiting Minkowski inclusion makes their affine average exactly the target affine plane. This proves the offset identity modulo the common direction space without assuming any globally affine original centroids or offsets.

Brunn--Minkowski with the common normalizer also proves that the positive support P_+ is lattice-convex. Intermediate integer bases cannot be omitted from the positive support.

## Cross-measure inequality and boundary compatibility

The limiting cross-base Brunn--Minkowski inequality is obtained using open epsilon neighborhoods for the source compact sets and a closed 2epsilon neighborhood of their compact Minkowski average. Lower Portmanteau at the sources and upper Portmanteau at the target have the required signs. This argument remains valid for sets lying in lower-dimensional limiting planes; one cannot instead intersect those exact sets with the prelimit bodies.

On a fixed anchored incidence the q-dimensional source balls lie in translates of the same Euclidean direction space, so their weighted sum is exactly a q-ball of radius epsilon times the weighted sum of the radii. No determinant enters. Optimizing the radius inequality under `sum lambda_i a_i=1` has the correct optimizer `a_i=b_i/S`, where `b_i=f_i^(1/(m-q))` and `S=sum lambda_i b_i`. The maximum is `S^((m-q)/m)`, yielding the exact cross-base density-root inequality. The q=0 case follows directly from the singleton mass inequality and does not use a fictitious derivative.

The source average of relative-interior support points is in the relative interior of the target support because it has an open q-dimensional ball inside the target. This validates density continuity at the point used in the calculation. Passing to arbitrary lift points by closing relative interiors is legitimate for every full relative-dimensional compact convex lift.

## One hidden Euclidean space, exact integer fibers, and Jacobians

The use of the first r axes of ONE added R^m is sufficient. Every actual anchored incidence has the same q and hence the same r=m-q, so all participating hidden spaces coincide literally. Unrelated fibers may use different first-axis subspaces without requiring a compatibility relation between them.

The x support direction and hidden y space are orthogonal. Intrinsic product Fubini therefore gives exactly `H_m(L_z)=integral f_z=p_z` and the required projected measure, including point-support fibers lifted to m-balls. The lift dimension is exactly q+r=m because the density is positive in the relative support interior. There is no base-dependent or graph-slope Jacobian.

Every point of the lifted convex hull over an integer base is a finite anchored combination. Combining repetitions and applying the proved inclusion shows that it belongs to the prescribed lift fiber. The reverse inclusion is by construction. Lattice-convexity of P_+ rules out any additional integer bases. Thus lower-dimensional integer fibers are not silently enlarged by the ambient hull.

## Saturated base reduction and depth scope

The base direction is rational, and its intersection with Z^k is a saturated sublattice. Translating by an integer base and extending a basis of this sublattice to an integer basis preserves the exact integer lattice. The unused base coordinates can then be deleted.

For the affine hull of the lift, the vertical kernel W contains every m-dimensional fiber direction, so m<=dim W<=2m. Choosing an affine section of the base projection and an isometry W->R^D gives a full relative-affine-hull body. On a fixed fiber this is a translation followed by an isometry, preserving H_m regardless of the total-dimensional Jacobian. The inverse section map, base embedding, and original x projection form one global affine map recovering the entire weak law.

A containing original closed halfspace pulls back to a containing closed halfspace, or to the entire source if its restriction is constant. The pointwise depth inequality follows with exact mass. It does not imply equality of maximal depths. The two perpendicular thin-triangle calibration has intrinsic lifted maximum 2/9 and projected weak-law maximum 1/4, exactly as stated; the verifier checks its intrinsic areas and constants.

This global weak-law representation is distinct from `historical context (not an accepted premise)`, whose stronger prelimit lower-semicontinuity statement retains complete normalized residual bodies in separate component blocks. The present theorem does not discard hidden prelimit halfspace information under an unsupported depth-continuity claim.
